ety.text: Latin aequālisbor. Middle English equal English equal From Middle English equal, from Latin aequālis. Doublet of aequalis and egal.

senses.d: The same in one or more respects.
ex: Near-synonyms: equivalent; see also Thesaurus:equal

senses.d: The same in value (status, merit, etc): having or deserving the same rights or treatment.
ex: We hold that all men are created equal and are thus equal under the law.
All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than the others.

senses.d: The same in all respects that matter practically; interchangeable, fungible, or (even sometimes) identical for practical purposes.
ex: Equal conditions should produce equal results.
All else being equal, we can expect this factor to have no discernible effect by itself.

senses.d: Exactly identical, having the same value.
ex: All right angles are equal.

senses.d: Fair, impartial.
ex: Are not my ways equal?
Thee, O Jove, no equall judge I deem.

senses.d: Adequate; sufficiently capable or qualified.
ex: This test is pretty tough, but I think I'm equal to it.
be equal to the task

senses.d: Not variable; equable; uniform; even.
ex: an equal movement
an equal temper

senses.d: Intended for voices of one kind only, either all male or all female; not mixed.
To be equal to, to have the same value as; to correspond to.
ex: Two plus two equals four.

senses.d: To make equivalent to; to cause to match.
ex: David equaled the water levels of the bottles, so they now both contain exactly 1 liter.

senses.d: To match in degree or some other quality, to match up to.
To have as consequence, to amount to, to mean.
ex: Losing this deal equals losing your job.
Might does not equal right.

senses.d: A person or thing of equal status to others.
ex: We're all equals here.
This beer has no equal.

senses.d: State of being equal; equality.
ex:
Thou that presum'st to weigh the world anew,
And all things to an equall to restore.

From earlier equale, from Latin aequālis, derived from aequus (“equal, even”).
Inherited from Old Spanish igual~egual (both common in the 13th century), from Latin aequālis. Cognate with English equal.
From Old Galician-Portuguese igual, ygual, from Latin aequālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin congener. First attested in 1861.

senses.d: An assertion that two expressions are equal, expressed by writing the two expressions separated by an equal sign; in mathematical problems, equations describe various essential aspects of the problem, each of which contributes to the resolution of the problem in part.

From Middle English equitee, equytee, from Old French equité, from Latin aequitās (“uniformity; impartiality; fairness”).

senses.d: Fairness, impartiality, or justice as determined in light of "natural law" or "natural right".
ex: “One of the staff said, ‘That’s fine, Delia. But what do wolves have to do with equity, justice and inclusion?’" Ms. Malone said.

senses.d: The power of a court of law having extra-statutory discretion, to decide legal matters and to provide legal relief apart from, though not in violation of, the prevailing legal code; in some cases, a court "sitting in equity" may provide relief to a complainant should the code be found either inapplicable or insufficient to do so.
ex:
1800, Lloyd Kenyon, 1st Baron Kenyon in Mayor, &c. of Southampton v. Graves (1800), 8 T. R. 592.
A Court of equity knows its own province.
A Court of equity interposes only according to conscience.

senses.d: A right which accrues to a party in a transaction because of the nature of the transaction itself, and which is exercisable upon a change of circumstances or conditions; in other words, an equitable claim.
The body of law which was developed in the English Court of Chancery, which Court had extra-statutory discretion, and is now administered alongside the common law of Britain.
Value of property minus liens or other encumbrances.
ex: I have a lot of equity in my house.

senses.d: Ownership, especially in terms of net monetary value of some business.
Ownership interest in a company as determined by subtracting liabilities from assets.
A player's expected share of the pot.
Equality
ex: What steps the Government are taking to help ensure equity of opportunity for people from low-income families.

ety.text: From Latin aequivalentem, accusative singular of aequivalēns, present active participle of aequivaleō (“to be equivalent, have equal power”). By surface analysis, equi- + -valent. Mostly displaced native Middle English efenmete (See evenmete).

senses.d: Similar or identical in value, meaning or effect; virtually equal.
ex: To burn calories, a thirty-minute jog is equivalent to a couple of hamburgers.
For now to serve and to minister, servile and ministerial, are terms equivalent.

senses.d: Of two sets, having a one-to-one correspondence.
ex: All enumerable sets are equivalent to each other, but not to any finite set.
Finite sets A and B are equivalent sets only when n(A) = n(B) i.e., the number of elements in A and B are equal.

senses.d: Relating to the corresponding elements of an equivalence relation.

Of two categories, (informally) such that one is essentially a relabeling of the other; (formally) related by a pair of functors such the composition of the one with the other is naturally isomorphic to the identity functor.
Having the equal ability to combine.
Of a map, equal-area.
Equal in measure but not admitting of superposition; applied to magnitudes.
ex: A square may be equivalent to a triangle.

senses.d: Anything that is virtually equal to something else, or has the same value, force, etc.
An equivalent weight.
To make equivalent to; to equal.

Any items used in equipping something or someone, for example things needed for an expedition or voyage.
ex: We need more gardening equipment if we want to properly landscape our yard, not just a rake and some gloves.
The sports shop sells different kits of famous clubs, and equipment from all kind of sports.

The state of a reaction in which the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are the same.
The state of a body at rest or in uniform motion in which the resultant of all forces on it is zero.

From French équiper (“to supply, fit out”), originally said of a ship, Old French esquiper (“to embark”); of Germanic origin, most probably from Old Norse skipa (“to man (a ship)”), from Proto-Germanic *skipōną (“to ship, sail, embark”). Compare with Middle High German schipfen, German schiffern, Icelandic skipa, Old English scipian. Doublet of ship.

senses.d: To supply with something necessary in order to carry out a specific action or task; to provide with (e.g. weapons, provisions, munitions, rigging).
ex:
1698-1699, Edmund Ludlow, Memoirs
Gave orders for equipping a considerable fleet.

senses.d: To dress up; to array; to clothe.
ex: The country are led astray in following the town, and equipped in a ridiculous habit, when they fancy themselves in the height of the mode.

senses.d: To prepare (someone) with a skill.
ex: I'm sorry, but I don't feel equipped to answer that kinda question yet.

senses.d: To equip oneself with (an item); to bring (equipment) into active use.
ex: Take it down from a distance with a magic spell, or equip your sword and attack it at close range.
